title: NASA's PRIMA Telescope Will Hunt for What JWST Can't See
summary:
The James Webb Space Telescope has dazzled the world with deep-space images since 2021. But there's a whole slice of the universe it simply cannot see: far-infrared light. Now NASA is designing a telescope to fill that gap.

The mission is called PRIMA — Probe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics. NASA announced this week that it's advancing to Phase B, the preliminary design and technology phase. If all goes to plan, PRIMA will launch no earlier than 2033 for a five-year mission.

Why does far-infrared matter? "The key science questions that PRIMA aims to address in relation to planet formation are to quantify the role of water in driving planet formation, and to determine the total gas masses and carbon and oxygen abundances in disks to reveal where exoplanets form," Meredith MacGregor, an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University, told Live Science. "We can't actually address these science questions with JWST because the spectral lines that are required are only in the far-infrared — longer wavelengths than JWST is sensitive to."

PRIMA will use a 5.9-foot (1.8-meter) telescope to study exoplanet origins, galaxy growth, and black hole evolution. It has a project cost cap of $1.2 billion — a fraction of JWST's $10 billion price tag. It's the first in a new class NASA calls Probe Explorers, designed to sit between flagship missions like JWST and smaller efforts. The program traces back to Explorer 1 in 1958 and has flown more than 100 missions.

"I'm most excited about the things I don't yet know," said Alberto Bolatto, an astronomer at the University of Maryland and a PRIMA co-investigator. Lee Armus of Caltech added that he's eager to see how powerful molecular outflows shape star formation and supermassive black holes.

NASA chose PRIMA over a competing X-ray concept after evaluating scientific merit, cost, and schedule. If it flies, NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory will manage the mission. The universe, it seems, still has colors we've never seen.
why_it_matters: Astronomy often advances when a new wavelength becomes observable — radio telescopes revealed the cosmic microwave background, and X-ray telescopes exposed black holes. If PRIMA flies, questions about where planets get their water and how galaxies grow would move from guesswork to measurement; if it is cancelled along the way, an entire generation of astronomers waits for the next opportunity.

background_read: Infrared light is the part of the spectrum just beyond red, and we feel it as heat. Earth's atmosphere absorbs most far-infrared light, so telescopes studying it must fly in space; NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope and the European Space Agency's Herschel Space Observatory both made infrared observations, but neither is still operating, leaving a gap that PRIMA is designed to fill.

The James Webb Space Telescope (a joint NASA, European and Canadian mission launched in 2021, and the most powerful infrared observatory ever flown) works mainly in near- and mid-infrared wavelengths. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (the agency's research centre in Pasadena, California, which builds and runs missions such as the Mars rovers) would manage PRIMA if it is built.

The Explorer programme (NASA's long line of small and medium science missions, which began with Explorer 1 in 1958, the first U.S. satellite and the mission that discovered the Van Allen radiation belts) has flown more than 100 missions. PRIMA's class, Probe Explorers, sits between small Explorer missions and billion-dollar flagships, which is why NASA compares scientific value against cost and schedule before choosing. Water, carbon monoxide, and other molecules important for planet formation glow most brightly at far-infrared wavelengths, which is why astronomers want a telescope built specifically for them.

perspectives.perspective: Positive: filling a real gap at a fraction of the price
perspectives.description: PRIMA targets wavelengths no current space telescope covers, and its $1.2 billion cap is roughly a tenth of JWST's cost, so NASA gets new science for far less money. The questions it would answer — how water and carbon arrive in planet-forming disks, how black holes grow — are central to understanding whether other worlds could support life. Astronomers also value the Probe Explorers idea of steady, mid-priced missions rather than rare giant ones.

perspectives.perspective: Critical: years away, with obvious risk
perspectives.description: A launch no earlier than 2033 means the mission is a decade of engineering and budget negotiations away, and many proposed telescopes are cut or delayed before they fly. Building infrared detectors and cooling systems sensitive enough for far-infrared work is technically hard, and history shows cost caps are often exceeded. Until it launches, the gap it is meant to fill stays open, and researchers must keep making do with limited data.

perspectives.perspective: Neutral: how space agencies sort ambitions by price
perspectives.description: Space science funding is a system of categories: small Explorers, mid-sized Probes, and flagships such as JWST. By placing PRIMA in the Probe class and picking it over a rival X-ray concept, NASA is balancing scientific merit, cost, and schedule rather than funding every good idea. This tiered approach, dating back to Explorer 1 in 1958, has kept a steady stream of missions flying even when the biggest projects run into trouble.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking: what a far-infrared sky could reveal
perspectives.description: If PRIMA reaches orbit, it would survey the cold, dusty parts of the universe where stars and planets are being born, and where much of the chemistry of life happens. The technology it develops could feed into later missions, just as earlier infrared telescopes paved the way for JWST. The real uncertainty is not what astronomers expect to see, but what they cannot yet predict — the surprises that new wavelengths usually bring.
